stem:
A 34-year-old sees her GP for postcoital bleeding on most occasions over four months. Pregnancy testing and chlamydia/gonorrhoea tests are negative. Speculum examination shows no visible cervical lesion, and a clinician-collected symptomatic co-test is HPV-negative with normal cytology. She has no intermenstrual bleeding and the symptom continues.

Which next step is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the co-test in 12 months, as both components are negative
options.explanation: A negative co-test lowers but does not remove the chance of significant pathology in a symptomatic woman; repeating it in a year leaves persistent bleeding unexplained.

options.label: B
options.text: Return her to routine five-yearly cervical screening
options.explanation: Screening intervals apply to asymptomatic people; persistent postcoital bleeding needs its cause found.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer for specialist gynaecological assessment of the bleeding
options.explanation: Persistent unexplained postcoital bleeding warrants specialist gynaecological assessment even after a negative co-test, because a small proportion of cancers are HPV-negative or missed on cytology.

options.label: D
options.text: Cauterise the cervix in general practice for presumed ectropion
options.explanation: No ectropion was seen and treating a presumed cause without specialist assessment could mask significant pathology.

options.label: E
options.text: Arrange colposcopy only if intermenstrual bleeding also develops
options.explanation: Persistent postcoital bleeding is itself the indication for assessment; waiting for another symptom delays diagnosis.

context: Persistent or recurrent postcoital bleeding warrants gynaecological assessment despite a negative co-test.
